# Book I

**All 48 propositions proved in Lean**: 46 as Euclid states them and 2 for a restricted statement ([I.40](40.md), [I.45](45.md)). 46 proofs follow Euclid's argument and 2 follow it with one step changed ([I.39](39.md), [I.40](40.md)); each page says how. In [I.23](23.md) one of our tacit rules already contains the proposition, and our proof rests on it, so the proof retraces Euclid's argument within our rules and does not establish the rule. In [I.2](02.md), [I.3](03.md) and [I.7](07.md) our tacit rules contain the propositions too, but our proofs never use those rules. [The overlap catalogue](../../docs/reports/overlaps.md) gives each. Our proofs of 29 propositions do not use the parallel postulate: I.1–I.28 and I.31. The first proof that does is I.29's, just where Euclid first calls on it.

Key to the table: ✅ proved. The Lean statement is *whole*, as Euclid states it; *restricted*, with hypotheses that leave out cases his words admit; or *in part*, leaving a clause to his words. Each page says how.

**From a triangle to Pythagoras.** Book I opens with an equilateral triangle on a given straight line and closes with Pythagoras' theorem and its converse (I.47, I.48). Heath sees three sections in it (vol. 1, p. 308): triangles, and how their sides and angles compare, up to I.26; parallels, from I.27, with the angles of a triangle (I.32) and the first parallelograms (I.33, I.34); and from I.35 on, areas that are equal without being congruent. Euclid holds his parallel postulate back until I.29, and so do our proofs. The decisions behind our statements, words and shared lemmas are gathered in [Book I's brief](../../docs/briefs/book-I.md).

**What each page holds.** First Euclid's enunciation and proof, in Sir Thomas Heath's 1908 translation, with a figure at a glance in Oliver Byrne's red, yellow and blue, and Euclid's own figure, both with Heath's letters. Heath's square brackets, such as [I. 3], are his references, pointing to the earlier result a step uses; Euclid himself seldom names one, for, as Heath remarks, "specific quotations of earlier propositions are rare in Euclid" (vol. 1, p. 83). Q. E. D. (*quod erat demonstrandum*, which was to be proved) closes a theorem, and Q. E. F. (*quod erat faciendum*, which was to be done) a problem. Then the Lean: Euclid's sentences are its `--` comments, word for word, with the Lean that carries them out beneath them, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`. A table of what the proof rests on follows; then the mishnah, our commentary, and a few books and papers to read alongside.

**What does the figure say?** That two circles cross, that a point lies between two others, which side of a straight line a point is on: Euclid reads all this off his figure, and our proofs say each one. We state each as a tacit rule, a named axiom. The rules follow System E, the list of what Euclid reads off his figures drawn up by Jeremy Avigad, Edward Dean and John Mumma, and every page's footer thanks them and the authors of LeanEuclid, which carried System E into Lean. "Intersection 5" and its kin are names from System E: an Intersection rule says when straight lines and circles must meet, and an Intersections rule lets us take a point where they do. Book Zero, in [`Elements/Figure`](../../Elements/Figure), is our small library of facts every figure needs, proved once from the tacit rules and citing no proposition.

**A straight line is whole.** In our foundations a straight line is the whole straight line, named by any two of its points (Postulate 1), so producing it usually costs nothing: the proofs of I.2 and I.5 do not use Postulate 2. Where a proof must cut off with I.3 from a straight line produced, as I.11 does, `produce_longer` first makes it long enough. Superposition, Euclid's picking up of a triangle, is one named rule, and only I.4 and I.8 call on it. That limit is a policy of ours, which the checks enforce: the rule asserts that a congruent triangle can be placed on a given ray and side, and as a construction principle it is stronger than System E's restricted rule ([its file](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean) says more). I.5 speaks of the equal sides produced, so a proof that wants only the angles at the base cites it through `Prop5.base`, which produces the sides anywhere. Where Euclid says "similarly", we write his argument once, for any letters, and use it in each place; where he gives one case and leaves the rest to the reader, Lean asks for every case, and we prove each.

**When must two straight lines meet?** Euclid first calls on Postulate 5 in I.29, and again in I.44. Our proofs of I.1 to I.28 never use it, nor does our proof of I.31, which draws its parallel with I.27 alone; every other proof from I.29 on rests on it. From I.37 on, Euclid often draws a parallel and names the point where it meets another straight line, reading the meeting off his figure. That a straight line meeting one of two parallels meets the other, Proclus states in his attempt to prove the postulate (Heath, vol. 1, p. 207), and under I.31 he infers from I.30 that the parallel through a point is unique (p. 316). Our `Prop30.meet` proves it from I.30, so wherever it is used the Lean cites I.30.

**Why does the Lean cite more?** The column "Heath's references" gives the propositions in Heath's brackets, and "Lean cites" those the Lean proof cites, which may be more, and now and then fewer; the table shows both. A bracket is Heath's pointer, not a reconstruction of the argument, and where there is none Euclid may still have had his reason. A shared step, a lemma proved once and used by many proofs, brings in the propositions it rests on, and the line under each table names those steps, with the propositions each brings in. The tacit rules are listed in full beneath it.
